records.notes: FR-040 boundary class for `build`: an image-reference configuration whose collection fields are all present and empty. An empty `features` map is the specific edge — it must produce the base image unchanged rather than an empty Feature layer or a failure.

Replaces the `--cache-to` half of `parity_build::buildkit-only-features` (res-build-tolerant-outcome). What this establishes is bounded and worth stating: deacon accepts the flag, passes it through, and still produces the image. What it does NOT establish is that anything was cached. The export type is `inline` on purpose: it is the ONE type buildx's default `docker` driver supports across Docker versions, so the case measures deacon rather than the runner. It was `type=local,dest=…` and that was the environment-dependent part — cache export needs the `docker-container` driver on older Docker, so on a CI runner the build produced no image at all and the case failed for a reason that had nothing to do with deacon (measured: it passes on Docker 29.6.2 / BuildKit v0.31.2, fails on GitHub `ubuntu-latest`, and Podman has no equivalent). Local export was never the claim either — even where it succeeded it wrote nothing to the destination. Pinning the reachable claim and naming the unreachable one is the honest shape; the legacy unit instead tolerated failure and, in its failure arm, accepted any of three substrings one of which (`outcome`) appears in normal JSON success output, so it could not fail either way.

Closes the Compose half of #440. The Compose build shape produces its feature-extended image through `resolve_compose_feature_image` rather than the Dockerfile path, and for that reason was outside #436's fix: it stamped no `devcontainer.metadata` at all, so an image a Compose `build` produced told a later `up` (or VS Code / Zed / envbuilder) nothing about the Features installed in it. The label is pinned WHOLE and by value rather than by presence: the entries are ordered (each installed Feature, then the config pick, lowest precedence first), and a presence check would pass on a label that recorded the wrong thing or dropped the Feature. `source: image` is pinned because a `build` leaves no container, so evidence captured from one would be answering a different question. Image pinned to alpine:3.19.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-build-compose-no-features-structured`. Building a Compose configuration has to resolve the SERVICE's build shape rather than the top-level one; the `-app` suffix on the reported image name is what shows which of the two was read, and `outcome` alone would not — a build of the wrong thing succeeds too. The image name's leading segment carries a workspace-derived hash and is deliberately left unpinned. Spec-expectation rather than differential because the structured rendering is reached by a flag the two CLIs spell differently, and the runner sends one argv to both sides.

The alignment half of the Dockerfile-plus-Feature build: both CLIs complete the build and report success. Kept separate from the `--image-name` case because the two CLIs do not share a tagging flag surface, so the overlay half cannot be a differential.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-build-dockerfile-cli-overlay-single-feature`. A Dockerfile build, a Feature layered on top of it, and a user-supplied `--image-name` — the exact combination in which this project once shipped a tag pointing at the PRE-Feature base. The assertion pins both halves in one ordered match: the reported image is the FEATURE-EXTENDED one (`deacon-devcontainer-features:…`), and the user's tag is among the tags applied to it. The stronger observation — running the tag and reading the Feature's marker — needs a `docker run` the declarative runner does not model, so the ordering constraint stands in for it and this note records the difference.

Closes #536, the coverage gap #417 left behind. `build` installs Features through the same resolver and the same layering pass as `up` (`commands/shared/feature_resolver::resolve_features_ordered`, `apply_features_and_lockfile`), and until now every `build` fixture declaring a Feature declared exactly ONE — so nothing would have reported the day `build`'s install order stopped matching `up`'s. The `devcontainer.metadata` label is where that order becomes a consumer's problem: it records one entry per installed Feature IN INSTALL ORDER, and a later `up`, VS Code or envbuilder reads the built image's label to learn what is in it.

The fixture separates the two ordering rules the way its `up` sibling `fx-up-feature-multi-dependency-order` does, on a Dockerfile base rather than an image reference so the case exercises `build`'s Dockerfile shape. The `features` map declares `./features/late` first and `./features/early` second; `late` carries `installsAfter: ["./features/early"]` (a soft edge) and `dependsOn: {"./features/pulled": {}}` (a hard edge to a Feature the configuration never names). Resolution must therefore INVERT the declaration and pull in a third Feature: `early` and `pulled` are both eligible in round one and commit in the §Round Stable Sort lexicographic order, then `late` commits in round two. Declaration order (`late, early`) and lexicographic order over the declared set (`early, late`) are both different sequences and neither contains `pulled` at all, so an implementation applying either rule fails here rather than passing by coincidence.

The assertion is POSITIONAL because it has to be. `jsonSubset` over an ARRAY is order-INSENSITIVE (`compare.rs::is_json_subset`), so an assertion over parsed label entries would pass for any permutation and would reproduce #417's vacuous claim one layer down. The label's value is a STRING, and pinning the whole string with `equals`-by-value inside the subset makes position the only thing it can match — the same reason `case-readconfig-dockerfile-declared-order-overlay` pins its array by index rather than by membership. The trailing config-pick entry is pinned alongside the three Feature entries, so the case also holds the entries' relative precedence (every installed Feature, then the configuration, lowest precedence first), and `--image-name ${IMAGE_TAG}` means the label is read off the image the USER's tag names — a tag left pointing at the pre-Feature base carries no Feature entries at all.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture, both CLIs, no divergence. deacon: `[{"id":"./features/early"},{"id":"./features/pulled"},{"id":"./features/late"},{"containerEnv":{…},"remoteUser":"root"}]`. Reference: the same four entries in the same order, differing only in JSON whitespace (`[ {…}, {…} ]`), which is the documented choice `bhv-container-metadata-label-serialization`. Both produced images were run and both report `early\npulled\nlate` from `/usr/local/share/conformance/install-order`, so the label's order is the order the installs actually ran in rather than only what a resolver reported.

SPEC-EXPECTATION RATHER THAN DIFFERENTIAL, deliberately. A `chan-image` differential over this label would need `wvr-container-metadata-label-serialization` to absorb the whitespace, and a tolerance is scoped to an observable PATH — tolerating `chan-image.labels.devcontainer.metadata` would excuse an ORDER difference on the same path, which is precisely the claim this case exists to make. A tolerance that blanks the thing being asserted is worse than no differential. The cross-CLI half of the ordering claim is carried where the tolerance does not reach: `case-up-feature-multi-dependency-order-differential` compares the marker sequence the same three Features write inside the container, through the same resolver `build` uses. One case rather than two for the same reason — the DECLARED-order rule (`overrideFeatureInstallOrder`) is already pinned at the install level by `case-up-feature-multi-declared-order` and at the resolution level by two `bhv-features-override-order-*` differentials, so a second `build` fixture would buy an image build on every gating run and no new information.

FR-034 build-time failure: the Dockerfile's `RUN` exits non-zero, so no image is produced. Both CLIs must fail, and the declared phase records WHERE — a build failure and a container-creation failure are the same exit code and different facts, which is the whole reason the phase is part of the record.

allowedDifferences.rationale: deacon stamps `org.deacon.configHash` on the image it builds; the reference sets no such label (measured against the pinned oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture). One named key in deacon's own namespace, never the `org.deacon.*` namespace as a whole. `devcontainer.metadata` is deliberately NOT tolerated alongside it: it was a deacon defect (#436), it is fixed, and the two sides now agree on that key — so a regression reappears here as a divergence instead of being excused.

records.notes: Ports `parity_build::with-build-args` (res-build-image-discovery). The fixture routes one `build.args` value into BOTH an image label and an environment variable, and the Dockerfile's `ARG` default is `default-not-passed` — so a build that silently dropped `build.args` produces an image that still exists and still carries the label, and is caught here by the VALUE (`default-not-passed` instead of `passed-from-config`) on two independent observables. That is the failure the legacy unit's substring check over `docker inspect` output was reaching for; this compares the whole image configuration between the CLIs instead. Everything agrees except `org.deacon.configHash`, which is tolerated (a deacon extension). `devcontainer.metadata` is NOT tolerated: deacon used to write it here unconditionally (a placeholder carrying `configHash`) where the reference writes it only when there is metadata to carry, and this fixture declares no Features and nothing in the configuration pick — so the defect showed up as a one-sided key. #436 closed it and neither side writes the label on this fixture now. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

allowedDifferences.rationale: deacon stamps `org.deacon.configHash` on the image it builds; the reference sets no such label (measured against the pinned oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture). One named key in deacon's own namespace, never the `org.deacon.*` namespace as a whole. `devcontainer.metadata` is deliberately NOT tolerated alongside it: it was a deacon defect (#436), it is fixed, and the two sides now agree on that key — so a regression reappears here as a divergence instead of being excused.

records.notes: Ports `parity_build::creates-discoverable-image` (res-build-image-discovery) and strengthens it. The legacy unit asked only whether an image carrying a unique label EXISTED after each side's build — a question answerable by a build that produced the wrong image entirely, as long as the label came along. This compares the produced image's whole configuration between the two CLIs: labels, environment, command, entrypoint, working directory. Made observable by the built-image capability: a `build` leaves an image and no container, so the container probe sees nothing and the case passes `--image-name ${IMAGE_TAG}` for a runner-assigned, per-side tag the observer inspects and the workspace reclaims. The image's own IDENTITY is not compared — the two sides build separately into different tags, so id/digests/tags differ by construction and say nothing about behavior. The label is a fixed literal rather than the legacy unit's PID-uniquified token: discovery is now by the assigned tag, so global uniqueness across concurrent runs is no longer the case's problem. TWO label keys once differed and are treated differently on purpose — `org.deacon.configHash` is a deacon extension and is tolerated by one named key; `devcontainer.metadata` was a deacon defect (#436) and is NOT tolerated, so this case reported it until the fix landed and reports any regression the same way. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Ports `parity_build::image-reference` (res-build-image-discovery), which is DEACON-ONLY — it never invoked the oracle — so a spec-expectation is its honest shape; a live-differential would claim cross-CLI agreement the unit never checked. Building from a plain image reference with a user tag and a `--label`, it pins the two halves the legacy unit checked and one it could not. (1) The reported `imageName` contains the tag the user asked for, asserted through the `<IMAGE_TAG>` token — the runner assigns a per-run, per-side tag, so the literal is unassertable and the token is what makes the claim expressible at all. (2) The produced IMAGE carries the `--label` value: the legacy unit inferred this from `docker images --filter label=…` returning a non-empty list, which proves only that SOME image matched; this reads the label off the image the build was told to write. `source: image` is pinned deliberately — without it the assertion would also pass on evidence captured from a container, and the whole point of this case is that a `build` leaves no container to capture.

Replaces `parity_build::output-json-format` (res-build-tolerant-outcome) by PINNING the outcome instead of porting the tolerance. The legacy unit branched on success/failure and, in its failure arm, accepted stdout or stderr containing any of "BuildKit is required", "outcome" or "Docker" — and a `--output-format json` build prints `outcome` in its normal success output, so the failure arm could pass on almost anything. An assertion that cannot fail is worse than no assertion. `--output type=docker,dest=…` is deterministic wherever a build can run at all: it exports to a path the case owns, so there is a single correct outcome to pin. The claim is deliberately the ARTIFACT, not the echo — `exportPath` alone repeats the flag back and would pass on a build that wrote nothing, so `chan-filesystem` asserts the tar exists. `<WORKSPACE>` is the path token; the case writes inside its own isolated workspace, which the runner reclaims. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Closes the `--output` half of #440, and is deacon-only (`--output` has no reference counterpart), so a spec-expectation is its honest shape. A `--push`/`--output` build used to hand its export straight to BuildKit, which left no local image to stamp — the exported image therefore carried NO `devcontainer.metadata`, having previously carried a wrong one. deacon now builds into the daemon, stamps, and exports from there, which is what makes the label observable at all: the export pass also loads, so the tag the case assigns names the STAMPED image and `chan-image` can read the label off it. `chan-filesystem` keeps the artifact claim from `case-build-output-export-tar` — a stamped image that was never exported would satisfy the label assertion alone. Image pinned to alpine:3.19.

Replaces the `--platform` half of `parity_build::buildkit-only-features` (res-build-tolerant-outcome). The legacy unit tolerated either outcome on the theory that BuildKit might be absent; it then asserted, only in the failure arm, that some error string appeared — so on any machine WITH BuildKit (every machine this suite runs on, and the default since Docker 23) it asserted nothing at all. `--platform` on the host's own architecture is deterministic, so this pins success and, through `chan-image`, that the flag produced a real image carrying the Dockerfile's label rather than merely being accepted. A genuinely BuildKit-less environment now fails this case loudly, which is the correct report — the suite's prerequisites are checked, not guessed at. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Replaces `parity_build::push-json-output` (res-build-tolerant-outcome). The legacy unit pushed to `localhost:5000` and branched on whether that happened to be reachable, so its assertion depended on the machine. `registry.invalid` is RFC 2606 reserved and resolves nowhere, so the push ALWAYS fails and there is one outcome to pin: exit 1, and a diagnostic that names the push as the failing step AND the target it failed on. Naming the target is what makes this case observe `bhv-build-push-target-selection` rather than merely assert it: deacon used to hand the push to BuildKit, which pushed every `-t` tag including deacon's internal `deacon-build:<hash>` — no registry component, so Docker Hub — and that push failed FIRST, so the reported target was the wrong one (#438). Restructuring the publish step for #440 made the push deacon's own and scoped it to the image names the user supplied, so the message now names `registry.invalid/conformance-push:latest`. The quoted target is deacon's own wording; the daemon's reason for the failure is BuildKit/daemon phrasing and is deliberately not pinned. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

A `features` value written as a bare string rather than an object, on `build`. This case carried a tolerance excusing an exit-code difference on the premise that "the reference accepts it and builds"; that premise is FALSE at oracle 0.87.0 and the tolerance was reported STALE the moment stale tolerances began failing. Re-measured: both CLIs exit 1. They reject for different reasons — deacon fails at config parse (`expected an object (map), found a string`), while the reference indexes the string as a legacy character-keyed feature map and fails with `Legacy feature '0' not supported` — but the observable exit code agrees, so there is nothing left to excuse and the class is `malformed`, not `reference-lenient`. The reference's LENIENCY toward this input is real on `read-configuration`, where it echoes the config instead of rejecting it; that is where `bhv-readconfig-wrong-type-features-rejected` and `wvr-wrong-type-features` still apply, and `case-errors-decl-wrong-type-features` pins the direction. Image pinned to alpine:3.18 (V18).

FR-040 unsupported class for `build`: a well-formed configuration naming an image reference no registry serves. Nothing about the document is wrong; the failure can only appear once something tries to obtain the image.

allowedDifferences.rationale: deacon stamps `org.deacon.configHash` on the image it builds; the reference sets no such label. Identical in scope and reasoning to the tolerance every other `chan-image` case in this suite carries — one named key in deacon's own namespace, never the `org.deacon.*` namespace as a whole — and re-measured against oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture. No other image key is tolerated here, so a regression on any of them surfaces as a divergence rather than being excused.

records.notes:
A Dockerfile whose first line is a `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` frontend directive, with an `ARG` consumed by `FROM` beneath it. The directive is meaningful only to BuildKit and only when it is the FIRST line — a CLI that rewrites, prepends to, or re-emits the Dockerfile (to inject Feature layers, or to resolve the `ARG`) can displace it, at which point Docker reads it as an ordinary comment and the build silently falls back to the classic frontend. The produced image is compared whole, so a frontend swap that changes anything observable about the image surfaces here.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0: the two images agree on everything except deacon's `org.deacon.configHash`, which is the extension every `chan-image` case in this suite already tolerates.

The fixture carries one authored `LABEL` for a reason worth recording. Without it the reference's image has NO labels at all (`Config.Labels` is `null`) while deacon's has its bookkeeping key, so the sides differ at the `labels` NODE rather than at a key inside it — the case's key-scoped tolerance could not reach it, and the run reported a STALE tolerance instead of a tolerated difference. A tolerance scoped to `<map>.<key>` is unreachable whenever the other side's whole map is absent.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures (#480, batch 1). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

Identical in scope and reasoning to the tolerance every other `chan-image` case in this suite carries — one named key in deacon's own namespace, never the `org.deacon.*` namespace as a whole — and re-measured against oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture. No other image key is tolerated here, so a regression on any of them surfaces as a divergence rather than being excused.

records.notes:
GREEN. `build.target` and `build.options` together, on a Dockerfile written to catch a wrong answer: three stages, a decoy BEFORE the named target and a decoy AFTER it, so an implementation that builds the last stage and one that builds the first both produce a DIFFERENT image rather than a failure.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0. `build.target` has always agreed — `/var/test-marker` carries `||test-content||` in both images, so both built the middle stage and skipped both decoys. `build.options` did NOT: deacon read it with `as_object()` and folded it into `build.args`, so the spec's ARRAY matched nothing and the `--label test_build_options=success` never reached the builder (#492). Fixed 2026-08-05 — `build.args` and `build.options` are distinct fields, the array is appended verbatim as discrete argv elements immediately after the `--build-arg` pairs (the reference's own position and semantics, measured), on BOTH the `build` and `up` Dockerfile paths. The ONE tolerance the case carries is the bookkeeping label every other `chan-image` case tolerates; `test_build_options` is deliberately not tolerated, so a regression on it surfaces.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures (#480, batch 1). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

Error-path tier, build stage, with the build ARGUMENT as the thing under test. The Dockerfile's `RUN` exits non-zero only when `CONF_FAIL=1` reaches it, and the configuration is the only place that value comes from — so a CLI that dropped `build.args` would SUCCEED here. The failure is therefore evidence that the argument was delivered, which the ordinary build-args case (`case-tier1-build-args-subst`, a configuration comparison) cannot supply: it observes the resolved document, not what the builder received. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0).

Error-path tier, build stage: `build.target` names a stage the Dockerfile does not define. Nothing about the document is wrong and BOTH CLIs read it without complaint — the target is a free-form string, and no reader can know which stages exist until the builder resolves the Dockerfile graph. That is the point: the failure is unreachable until after the stage where the reference is most lenient, which is exactly where parity used to stop comparing. Both sides fail (verified against oracle 0.87.0 in an isolated workspace).

GREEN since [#556](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/556) closed; RED on purpose before it, and the assertions below are BYTE-IDENTICAL to the day it landed — the case turned green on the fix, not on an edit. `build --frozen-lockfile` on a workspace with NO lockfile must refuse: the flag's whole contract is "resolution may not change the lockfile", and there is no lockfile for resolution to agree with.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture, BEFORE the fix. The reference exits 1 before building anything, prints `{"outcome":"error","message":"Lockfile does not exist."}` and leaves the workspace clean. deacon exited 0, built the Feature-extended image, and WROTE `.devcontainer-lock.json` (327 bytes) — the precise inverse of what the flag asks for. The cause was not subtle and was admitted in the source: `commands/build/mod.rs`'s `BuildArgs` documented `no_lockfile` / `frozen_lockfile` as "not yet consumed by `build`'s lockfile-writing path", so both flags were parsed, threaded, and then dropped. A modelled flag accepted and then ignored is the silent-fallback shape constitution IV rules out — the same class as #492 (`build.options`), one surface over.

AFTER: deacon exits 1 with `Lockfile does not exist.` and writes nothing. The fix routes `build` through the SAME decision `up` already made rather than giving it a second one — the skip / semantic-compare / write policy now lives in `commands/shared/lockfile` and both subcommands reach it, so a lockfile's bytes and its fate never depend on which subcommand resolved the Features. The refusal happens BEFORE the build, matching where the reference throws (its `writeLockfile` is reached from `generateFeaturesConfig`, which runs before the image build), and it is gated on the configuration DECLARING Features for the same reason — that early return is why `build --frozen-lockfile` on a featureless config with no lockfile exits 0 on both CLIs.

TWO channels, and both are load-bearing. The exit code alone would pass the day someone made `build` fail for an unrelated reason; the filesystem claim is the one that says the refusal happened BEFORE anything was written.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures (#480, batch 2 — the lockfile family). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

GREEN since [#556](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/556) closed; RED on purpose before it, with assertions unchanged. The same defect as `case-build-upstream-lockfile-frozen-missing` seen through the other flag, and the half that CANNOT be caught by an exit code: both CLIs exit 0, both produce an image, and the only observable difference was a file one of them wrote that the user asked it not to write.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture: the reference build succeeds and `.devcontainer-lock.json` is ABSENT afterwards. BEFORE the fix deacon's build succeeded and the file was PRESENT (327 bytes, the resolved `git:1.3.2` entry); AFTER, it is absent. Two flags, one cause — `build` parsed `--no-lockfile` / `--frozen-lockfile` and never consulted either.

Both cases are kept rather than merged into one, because the two flags have opposite correct outcomes (refuse vs succeed-and-write-nothing) and a fix that wired only one of them would leave the other silently broken. The shared `LockfilePolicy` enum is what makes that impossible to get half-right: one value decides both. Measured alongside: `--no-lockfile` also leaves an EXISTING lockfile byte-identical on both CLIs.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures (#480, batch 2 — the lockfile family). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

GREEN. `--no-lockfile` and `--frozen-lockfile` ask for contradictory things — ignore the lockfile entirely, and require it to be present and unchanged — so naming both is a user error rather than a precedence question, and the reference rejects it rather than picking a winner. Upstream drives this from three parameterised tests (the second flag is `--frozen-lockfile`, `--experimental-frozen-lockfile` or `--experimental-lockfile`); the graduated pair is the one both CLIs share, so it is the one measured here.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0: both exit 1, and both leave the workspace byte-identical — the rejection happens at argument validation, before either CLI touches Docker, a registry or the filesystem. So the case needs no daemon — and it is `resourceGroup: fs-heavy` anyway, which is the group that isolates a workspace WITHOUT touching Docker. `none` was the obvious choice and is the wrong one, and the reason was found by perturbing this very case: a `none` case runs against the COMMITTED fixture directory, so when the watched-to-fail run dropped `--no-lockfile` from the argv, the surviving `--frozen-lockfile` stopped being rejected, deacon built for real, and a stray `.devcontainer-lock.json` appeared in `parity/fixtures/fx-upstream-lockfile-no-lockfile/` — an untracked file that would have silently changed what the OTHER cases on that fixture measure, which is exactly the failure #423 documented for `fx-upgrade-overlay-lockfile`. A `build` or `up` operation must never run un-isolated, however certain one is that today's argv writes nothing: the argv is one edit away from writing. The `absent` filesystem claim is kept as the second line of defence.

`chan-stderr` is deliberately NOT declared. Both CLIs say the same sentence (`--no-lockfile and --frozen-lockfile are mutually exclusive.`), but the reference prepends its entire `yargs` usage block, so comparing the stream would report a divergence about help-text formatting and say nothing about the behaviour. The exit code plus the assertion is the whole claim.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures (#480, batch 2 — the lockfile family). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

GREEN since [#571](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/571) closed; **RED ON PURPOSE** from the day it landed until then, with its assertions UNCHANGED across the fix. It stated the fixed behaviour on both channels from the start, so it turned green on the code and not on a case edit — the pattern batch 2's three red cases established.

It stays `live-differential`, and `case-build-lockfile-integrity-pin-enforced` is its `spec-expectation` twin: identical assertions, identical fixture, different lane. This one keeps confirming run by run that the reference still agrees; that one gates.

The claim is the one the lockfile exists for: **`integrity` is a content pin, and a Feature whose content does not match it must not be installed.** `parity/spec/113500f4/devcontainer-lockfile.md` states it as a goal in so many words — "Improved security by detecting when a feature's release artifact changes after its checksum was first recorded in the lockfile ('trust on first use')" — so this is not a spec-silent surface where the reference is merely the authority. Both the spec and the reference say deacon is the wrong side.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-upstream-lockfile-oci-integrity`, whose committed `.devcontainer-lock.json` names the CORRECT `resolved` digest for `ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/git:1.3.2` and a deliberately wrong `integrity` differing from it in one hex character. The reference exits 1 with `{"outcome":"error"}` (`Could not resolve Feature manifest for 'ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/git:1.3.2'` → `ERR: Feature … could not be processed`) and leaves the file byte-unchanged. BEFORE the fix deacon exited 0, built the Feature-extended image, and **overwrote the corrupted `integrity` with the correct digest** — so a tampered lockfile was not merely ignored, it was silently repaired, and the next `git diff` was the only thing that would ever have said so. AFTER, deacon exits 1 without fetching the Feature's content and leaves the file byte-unchanged, because the pin is now the manifest LOOKUP KEY on deacon's side too.

The control that makes this a measurement rather than an inference: the SAME fixture with the correct `integrity` (`fx-upstream-lockfile-frozen`'s committed lockfile) builds successfully on the reference, exit 0. One hex character is the whole difference between the two runs.

Why the reference fails is transcribed from the bundle rather than guessed, because "it verified a checksum" would have been wrong. `integrity` is the LOOKUP KEY: `kb(ctx, ref, integrity)` → `ji`, which does `let r = e.version; t && (r = t)` and requests `…/v2/<path>/manifests/<integrity>` instead of the tag, then re-checks the returned `docker-content-digest` against it (`if (r && C !== r) throw new Error('Digest did not match for …')`). A wrong `integrity` therefore cannot resolve at all. That shape is now deacon's: `FeatureFetcher::fetch_feature_pinned` substitutes the pin for the tag in the manifest URL and re-checks the digest that comes back. Before the fix `oci/fetcher.rs` computed the manifest digest only to RECORD it, and `crates/core/src/lockfile.rs` had no consumer of `integrity` outside `--frozen-lockfile`'s document comparison and `outdated`/`upgrade` reporting.

`--frozen-lockfile` is deliberately NOT in the argv, and is the near-miss worth naming: with it, deacon DOES exit 1 here (`Lockfile does not match.`), because the freshly-resolved entry differs from the corrupted one. That is a comparison of two documents, not a verification of content, and it is opt-in — the default path, which is what upstream's test exercises and what a user gets, checks nothing.

The `chan-file-content` assertion pins the lockfile's exact committed bytes rather than declaring a bare differential, for the same reason the exit code carries an `equals`: a differential alone passes when both sides are equally wrong, and this case's second half is precisely that deacon WROTE where the reference did not. `chan-stderr` is not declared — the two diagnostics say the same thing in different sentences, and comparing them would report prose.

Mined from the reference CLI's own e2e fixtures at `v0.87.0` ([#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480), batch 3 — the item batch 2 named "the most landable of the deferrals" and could not land because it had not been measured). Vendored from devcontainers/cli v0.87.0; see the fixture's UPSTREAM.md for the source path and every adaptation.

The GATING half of `case-build-upstream-lockfile-oci-integrity`, which asserts the same two things about the same fixture and is `live-differential` — so `lane_of` sends it to `parity_docker` here and to `parity_differential` there. The pairing is the one `case-outdated-malformed-lockfile-rejected` / `-differential` established, and the reason for it is sharper on this behaviour than on that one: a regression that stopped honouring `integrity` would silently reinstate a security defect ([#571](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/571)), and the nightly gates nothing. This case runs in the release gate and in every Docker-provisioned profile; its differential twin keeps confirming, run by run, that the reference still agrees.

Nothing about the ASSERTIONS differs between the two — that is deliberate. The re-laning rule is that a case may move lanes but may never have what it claims rewritten to fit the new lane, and the claims here were absolute from the day the red case landed (`equals: 1`, and the lockfile's exact bytes), so they need no adaptation to stand without an oracle beside them.

The `chan-file-content` pin is the load-bearing half. deacon's pre-#571 failure was not that it exited 0 — it was that it exited 0 having REWRITTEN the corrupted `integrity` to the digest it had just fetched, so the tampering was repaired and the only witness was a `git diff` nobody ran. An implementation that refused but still rewrote the file would satisfy the exit code alone.

The BOUNDARY of the `integrity` pin, on the same tampered fixture that proves the pin exists. `--no-lockfile` means "do not READ", not merely "do not write": the reference computes `A.noLockfile ? {lockfile: undefined} : await fI(t)` and threads that `undefined` into every Feature lookup, so a `--no-lockfile` run resolves by tag and a corrupted lockfile cannot fail it.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on this exact workspace: the same fixture that exits 1 on a plain `build` exits 0 under `--no-lockfile` and produces a Feature-extended image. One flag is the whole difference between the two runs, which is what makes this a measurement of the carve-out rather than of the Feature.

It is here because a pin is the kind of fix that is easy to over-apply, and an over-applied one is invisible: it looks like security. Without this case the cheapest wrong implementation — read the lockfile unconditionally — passes every other lockfile case in the suite, since the only one that would notice is a `--no-lockfile` run against a lockfile that disagrees with reality, and that combination existed nowhere until this case.

`--output-format json` is in the argv because `chan-structured-output` is: deacon's `build` prints a human summary otherwise, and the channel reports `stdout was not valid JSON` rather than anything about the flag under test — which is how this case first ran red.

Three channels, each load-bearing. `chan-exit-code: 0` is the carve-out itself. `chan-structured-output` pinning `outcome: success` is what makes that 0 mean "the image was built" rather than "something quietly declined to happen". `chan-file-content` pinning the CORRUPTED bytes is the write half of the same flag: a run that resolved by tag and then repaired the lockfile would satisfy both other assertions while doing the thing `--no-lockfile` exists to prevent — and repairing it is exactly what deacon did on every path before [#571](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/571).

The other consequence of reading the lockfile at all ([#571](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/571)). Once `integrity` PINS resolution, a lockfile that cannot be parsed is not a cosmetic problem to be papered over by rewriting it — it is an input the run depends on and cannot have.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-lockfile-unreadable`: the reference exits 1 with `{"outcome":"error","message":"Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 2 …"}` and leaves the file byte-unchanged. Its `readLockfile` (`fI`) swallows only `ENOENT`; a `SyntaxError` carries no `.code`, so the `throw e` rethrows it. BEFORE the fix deacon exited 0, built the Feature-extended image, and REPLACED the unparseable file with a freshly-resolved lockfile — the same silent repair the tampered-`integrity` case documents, reached by a different corruption.

`spec-expectation` + `fs-heavy` puts this in the HERMETIC lane, and that is a claim rather than a convenience: the refusal happens while reading a local file, before deacon touches a registry or a daemon. `parity_hermetic` re-runs its own drivers inside a fresh network namespace, so a regression that moved this refusal after the Feature fetch or the base-image build would not merely fail the assertion — it would fail to reach it at all, loudly. `none` would have been the wrong group for the reason `case-build-upstream-lockfile-flags-mutually-exclusive` records: a `none` case runs against the COMMITTED fixture directory, and one edit to this argv is all it would take for a real build to write a `.devcontainer-lock.json` into `parity/fixtures/`.

`chan-stderr` is deliberately not declared. Both CLIs report the position of the offending character, but they are two different JSON parsers describing the same byte, and comparing them would report a difference about serde vs V8 rather than about the behaviour. The exit code plus the file's surviving bytes is the whole claim — and the bytes matter more than the code here, since the defect this replaces was a successful run that overwrote them.

jsonSubset.message: Cannot use --platform with Docker Compose configurations

records.notes:
A Compose configuration cannot honour `--platform`: the platform belongs to a single image build and a Compose project builds whatever its services declare. Both CLIs refuse rather than accept-and-ignore, which is the failure mode that matters — a flag taken and dropped is the silent-fallback shape constitution IV rules out, and it is invisible to an exit code alone.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-compose`: both CLIs exit 1 and both print an error document. The WORDING differs (`--platform or --push not supported.` against deacon's `Cannot use --platform with Docker Compose configurations`), and that is exactly why this is `spec-expectation` rather than `live-differential`: a differential on the result document would report a message-text disagreement forever and would need a tolerance to say nothing more than 'they phrase it differently'. Pinning deacon's own document says more and costs less. deacon's wording names the flag AND the configuration shape that cannot take it; the reference's names two flags, only one of which was passed.

HERMETIC on purpose. The refusal is a pre-flight decision about the resolved configuration, so it must happen before any daemon contact — VERIFIED by running it with `DOCKER_HOST` pointed at a socket that does not exist, where it still exits 1 with the same document. A regression that moved the check after the Compose project was created would fail this case inside `parity_hermetic`'s network namespace rather than passing on a technicality.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should fail with docker-compose and --platform not supported'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

jsonSubset.message: Cannot use --cache-to with Docker Compose configurations

records.notes:
The second half of the same rule as `case-build-upstream-compose-platform-refused`, kept as its own case because the two flags are refused by different code and a fix that wired only one would leave the other silently accepted. Upstream keeps them apart for the same reason.

The `chan-filesystem` assertion is what makes this more than an exit code: `--cache-to type=local,dest=…` names a directory the run would CREATE, so a CLI that refused only after handing the flag to the builder would leave it behind. Refusing and writing nothing are two claims and only one of them is an exit code.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-compose`: both CLIs exit 1, both print an error document, neither writes the destination. Wording differs (`--cache-to not supported.`), which is why this pins deacon's document rather than comparing the two — see the sibling case for the argument. HERMETIC, verified with `DOCKER_HOST` pointed at a nonexistent socket.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should fail with docker-compose and --cache-to not supported'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

`--push` and `--output` are both destinations for the built image and they are mutually exclusive: one hands the result to a registry, the other writes it to a path. Taking both would mean silently picking one.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-flags`: both CLIs exit 1 before building anything and neither writes the export. deacon says `Cannot use both --push and --output`, the reference `--push true cannot be used with --output.` — the same refusal in different words, so `spec-expectation` for the reason given in `case-build-upstream-compose-platform-refused`.

`chan-filesystem` carries the half the exit code cannot: refusing is one claim, writing nothing on the way out is another, and a CLI that validated the combination only after starting the export would satisfy the first while failing the second. HERMETIC — the check is pure argument validation, verified with `DOCKER_HOST` pointed at a nonexistent socket.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should fail with --push true and --output'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

`build` on a workspace with no `devcontainer.json` fails with exit 1 and names the file it could not find. Nothing covered this for `build`: the existing no-config cases belong to `read-configuration` (two), `doctor` and `down`, and `build` reaches config resolution by its own path.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-errors-missing-config`: both CLIs exit 1 and both name the absolute path of the document they looked for. The reference puts that on STDOUT as `{"outcome":"error","message":"Dev container config (…) not found."}`; deacon puts the diagnostic on stderr and prints nothing on stdout even under `--output-format json`. That difference is [#594](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/594), tracked by its own row — this case deliberately asserts only the half that is correct today, so it is green from the day it lands and stays green after the JSON gap closes.

HERMETIC: config resolution fails before any daemon contact, verified with `DOCKER_HOST` pointed at a nonexistent socket. The lane is a claim, not a convenience — a regression that contacted the daemon before reading the workspace would fail here rather than pass.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should fail with "not found" error when config is not found' and 'should fail gracefully when no workspace-folder and no config in current directory'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

`--image-name` is repeatable: every name given becomes a tag on the one built image, and the result document lists them in the order they were passed. Every other `build` case in the suite passes the flag exactly once, so the repeatable half was carried by the argument parser alone.

The tag ORDER is the claim, and it needs `jsonEquals` to express — `jsonSubset` treats an array as an order-insensitive 'contains', so a subset assertion here would pass on a CLI that reversed the list. The document has exactly two keys, which is what makes an equality assertion on the whole of it possible.

The tokenized `${IMAGE_TAG}` is deliberately the SECOND name rather than the first. `chan-image` inspects only the tag the runner issued, so putting it last is what proves the later names are real tags on a real image and not just echoes in the result document — the exact failure this project has shipped once before, where `--image-name` was reported correctly and pointed at the pre-Feature base. A case that asserted only the array would pass on a CLI that reported two names and tagged one.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-flags`: both CLIs exit 0 and both report `imageName` as the two names in order; `docker images` shows one tag per name.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, the three 'should succeed with multiple --image-name parameters …' cases), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

A `--cache-from` reference that does not resolve is a MISS, not an error: the build proceeds and produces the image. This is the shape CI actually runs — a pipeline names the cache image for the target branch, and on a first build for a new branch that image does not exist yet. Upstream's own comment on the test says so ('example scenario: CI builds for PRs'), which is why the case is worth having rather than being filed under 'flag accepted'.

The reference `ghcr.io/devcontainers/notFound` is kept VERBATIM from upstream and is deliberately not repinned: the claim is about a name that cannot be resolved, so a name that resolves would destroy it, and unlike a Feature reference there is no third-party CONTENT here to go stale — the only thing the case depends on is the repository continuing not to exist.

`chan-image` is what stops this from passing vacuously. Exit 0 and `outcome: success` are also what a CLI that silently skipped the build would print; the label comes from the Dockerfile, so it is evidence an image was actually built.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-flags`: both CLIs exit 0, both report success, both produce the image. `docker-shared` rather than hermetic — the case reaches ghcr.io by construction, and a Docker-grouped case already has network.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should execute successfully with valid image config and extra cacheFrom'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

With no `--workspace-folder`, `build` resolves the configuration from the CURRENT DIRECTORY. This is the shape a developer types — `cd` into the project, run `deacon build` — and every other `build` case in the suite passes the flag explicitly, so nothing covered it.

It costs nothing to express: the runner already invokes each operation with its cwd set to the case's isolated workspace, so OMITTING the flag is the whole test. That is also the case's one fragility, recorded here because it is invisible in the argv — if the runner ever stops anchoring cwd to the workspace, this case starts failing for a reason that has nothing to do with `build`. The sibling `case-exec-default-workspace-folder` (batch 4) carries the same note for the same reason.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-flags`: both CLIs exit 0 and build the image from the cwd's configuration. The IMAGE NAMES differ by construction and are not compared — deacon derives `deacon-build:<hash>` and the reference `vsc-<folder>-<hash>` — which is one more reason this is `spec-expectation`.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should use current directory for build when no workspace-folder provided'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

RED ON PURPOSE — [#592](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/592). `--platform` is a BuildKit capability: the legacy builder cannot target a platform at all. Asked for both `--buildkit never` and a platform, a CLI has exactly two honest answers, and building for the WRONG platform while reporting success is neither.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-build-flags`, on an aarch64 host: the reference exits 1 with `{"outcome":"error","message":"--platform or --push require BuildKit enabled."}` and builds nothing. deacon exits 0, prints `{"outcome": "success"}`, and produces an image — for the HOST architecture, because the legacy builder ignored the flag. The user asked for `linux/amd64` and got arm64 with a zero exit: the silent-fallback shape constitution IV rules out, and the same class as #492 (`build.options` parsed and dropped) and #556 (the lockfile flags parsed and dropped) one surface over.

The assertion is the exit code alone, and that is deliberate rather than lazy. The two CLIs word the refusal differently, so declaring `chan-structured-output` would make the differential report a message-text disagreement forever; the wording is pinned instead by the `spec-expectation` sibling that lands with the fix. `nonZero` rather than `equals: 1` because what this case is about is REFUSING — the specific code is the fix's business.

`live-differential` puts it in the nightly, which gates nothing, so it can be red from the day it lands. The precedent is `case-build-upstream-lockfile-frozen-missing`: the assertion here is what turns green on the fix, and it must not be edited when that happens.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should fail with BuildKit never and --platform'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.

RED ON PURPOSE — [#593](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/593). `--platform` on an IMAGE-reference configuration, as opposed to the Dockerfile configuration `case-build-platform-flag` already covers. The two take different code paths in deacon and only one of them works.

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-up-basic`, on an aarch64 host, with `--platform linux/amd64` (foreign there): the reference exits 0 and produces a genuine amd64 image (`docker inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}'` says `amd64`). deacon exits 1 with `failed to resolve source metadata for docker.io/library/deacon-build-run:<n>-0: pull access denied`. deacon builds the base as a local intermediate tag and then does `FROM deacon-build-run:<n>-0` under `--platform`; the local tag exists only for the host platform, so BuildKit goes looking for the foreign variant in a registry that has never heard of it. The Dockerfile path does not chain that way and cross-builds correctly — VERIFIED in the same session, same host, `--platform linux/amd64` on `fx-build-flags` exits 0 and produces an amd64 image.

THE PLATFORM VALUE IS ARCH-RELATIVE AND THE CASE IS ONLY MEANINGFUL WHERE THE REQUESTED PLATFORM IS FOREIGN. It is written `linux/arm64` because the lane it runs in — the nightly, on `ubuntu-latest` — is x86_64, where arm64 is the foreign one; on an aarch64 developer machine this case is native and therefore vacuous, and the measurement above is the mirror image of it. No emulation is required either way: the fixture is `{"image": "alpine:3.19"}` with no Features and no `RUN`, so nothing foreign is ever EXECUTED — the failure is at reference resolution, before any instruction runs. Recorded because a case that is vacuous on some substrates and not others must say so out loud.

The exit code alone, for the same reason as the sibling above: the image NAMES differ between the two CLIs by construction, so a document or image comparison would diverge on something this case is not about. The `spec-expectation` sibling that pins the produced image's architecture lands with the fix.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.build.test.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should succeed (image) with supported --platform'), [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480) batch 5.
